description: All thirteen spec life factors — abuse, access, economic, environment, family, identity and more.
content_html:
What Is a Life Factor?

A life factor is a condition or circumstance — not a choice, but a given — that shapes how a person grows, develops, and experiences health. The spec identifies thirteen named life factors, grouped broadly into areas covering relationships, access to services, economic conditions, the living environment, personal health, and identity. Health and social care practitioners need to understand these factors because many of the individuals they support have been significantly affected by them.

Life factors differ from lifestyle choices (such as diet or exercise, covered in the next lesson). A child does not choose their family structure, their neighbourhood, or whether they experience abuse — these are factors imposed on them. Recognising this distinction matters in practice: a key-worker in a residential care home who understands the life factors a resident has faced can provide more empathetic, person-centred support.

Abuse

Abuse is one of the most damaging life factors an individual can experience. The spec identifies seven distinct types: physical abuse (causing bodily harm), emotional abuse (persistent criticism, humiliation, rejection or threats), sexual abuse (any sexual act without consent), verbal abuse (using words to belittle, demean or control), neglect (failure to meet basic physical or emotional needs), coercive control (a pattern of behaviour that controls, threatens or frightens a person), and financial abuse (misusing or stealing someone’s money or assets).

Key Fact

The seven types of abuse are: physical, emotional, sexual, verbal, neglect, coercive control, and financial. Any form of abuse has profound effects across all PIES domains — physical injury, intellectual disruption, emotional trauma, and social withdrawal are all documented consequences. Practitioners have a duty to report concerns to safeguarding leads.

Each type of abuse affects PIES development in interconnected ways. Neglect during infancy, for example, disrupts attachment formation (emotional), impairs brain development (intellectual), delays physical growth, and limits socialisation (social). Coercive control in an adult relationship can affect physical health (through enforced isolation or withheld medication), intellectual development (restricted access to education or work), emotional wellbeing (persistent fear and low self-esteem), and social contacts (enforced isolation from friends and family).

Access to Services

Access to services is a significant life factor because unequal access produces unequal outcomes. The spec highlights immunisations and screening programmes, early years services (children’s centres, nurseries), youth services, and day centres. Children who miss immunisations face higher disease risk; adults who cannot access mental health services may deteriorate without support; older adults who have no access to a day centre may face severe social isolation.

Barriers to access include geography (rural areas with fewer services), financial cost (transport, prescription charges), language barriers, disability, and lack of knowledge about what services exist. The Marmot Review (2010) highlighted that inequalities in access to services are a major driver of health inequalities across the lifespan in the UK.

Economic Factors

Economic factors — including employment, income, wages, benefits, savings, and material possessions — are among the most powerful determinants of health. The spec distinguishes absolute poverty (lacking the basic necessities for survival) from relative poverty (having significantly less than the average standard of living in your society).

Poverty affects PIES across the lifespan. Children growing up in low-income households are more likely to have poor nutrition, live in damp or overcrowded housing, attend underfunded schools, and experience the emotional stress of financial insecurity — all of which affect their cognitive development and social participation. Adults in unemployment face not only financial hardship but loss of routine, social contacts, and sense of purpose, which can significantly damage emotional wellbeing. The standard of living and quality of housing are directly linked to physical health outcomes — cold, damp homes increase respiratory illness; overcrowding increases infection spread.

Educational Experiences

Educational experiences — including the quality of schooling, experiences of bullying, and the influence of peers — shape intellectual, emotional, and social development significantly. A child who is bullied at school may avoid attendance, miss learning, experience anxiety and low self-esteem, and withdraw from peer groups — affecting all four PIES domains. A child who receives strong, inclusive educational support is more likely to develop confidence, communication skills, and academic achievement that open future employment opportunities.

Living Environment

The physical environment in which a person lives is a life factor they typically do not control. Relevant environmental factors include: access to green space (linked to mental well-being and physical activity), overcrowding (affects sleep, stress levels, and infection risk), unsafe conditions (structural hazards in housing, dangerous neighbourhoods), and pollution (both air pollution, which damages respiratory health, and noise pollution, which disrupts sleep and concentration).

Family and Relationships

Family structure and parenting style are significant life factors. The spec names several family types: nuclear (two parents and children), extended (including grandparents or other relatives), single-parent, step, foster, adoptive, and same-sex parent families. No family type is inherently better for development — the quality of relationships within the family matters more than its structure.

Parenting style is a particularly well-researched influence on child development. The spec identifies four main styles:

Authoritative: high warmth, clear rules with explanation. Associated with positive outcomes: children tend to develop high self-esteem, good social skills, and academic confidence. Authoritarian: strict rules, low warmth, obedience demanded without explanation. Can produce well-behaved children but also lower self-esteem and limited autonomy. Neglectful: low warmth, low control; the parent is largely disengaged. Associated with poor outcomes across all PIES domains. Indulgent: high warmth, low rules; the child gets what they want without learning boundaries. Can lead to difficulties with self-regulation and following rules in school and later life.

Gender, Sexuality, and Long-Term Conditions

Gender and sexuality can be life factors where they expose individuals to discrimination, prejudice, or exclusion. LGBT+ individuals may face stigma in schools, workplaces, and some community or family settings, which can significantly affect emotional wellbeing, social development, and mental health.

Long-term and life-limiting conditions are also named life factors. These include congenital conditions (present from birth), genetic conditions, chronic illness (long-term conditions such as Type 1 diabetes or epilepsy), and comorbidity (having more than one long-term condition at the same time). Comorbidity is increasingly common in older adults and significantly increases the complexity of care needs.

Culture and race are life factors where they shape an individual’s experiences of discrimination and prejudice. Ethnic minority individuals in the UK are statistically more likely to experience socioeconomic disadvantage, housing inequality, and healthcare disparities — all of which create additional barriers to health. Learning disabilities (including conditions on the autism spectrum) and behavioural disorders (such as ADHD) affect intellectual and social development. Sensory impairments — hearing and sight loss — limit access to information, education, and social participation without appropriate support from practitioners and services.

Key Fact

The spec rewards linkage: economic disadvantage doesn’t just mean ‘less money’ — it links to nutrition, housing quality, exposure to stress, and access to enrichment activities, all of which delay or disrupt PIES milestones in specific named ways.
exam_tip_html: Questions on life factors commonly use a case-study format and ask you to ‘identify’ or ‘explain’ a life factor affecting the named individual. The most common mistake is confusing a life factor with a lifestyle choice — remember: a life factor is something the individual does not choose (their family, their neighbourhood, a disability), while a lifestyle choice is a behaviour they elect (their diet, whether they smoke). For 3-mark ‘Explain’ questions, name the life factor, state its effect, and add a ‘because’ or ‘this means that’ to develop it into a third mark. Do not list multiple factors without developing any — depth beats breadth for this question type.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The spec names thirteen distinct life factors: abuse (seven types), access to services, economic factors, educational experiences, living environment, family and relationships (including four parenting styles), culture and race, gender and sexuality, long-term conditions, learning disabilities, behavioural disorders, mental health, and sensory impairments.
  • Life factors are conditions individuals are born into or find themselves in — not choices. They affect all four PIES domains and often interact: poverty limits access to services, which worsens health outcomes, which increases economic burden.
  • Recognising life factors helps practitioners provide person-centred care — understanding why an individual’s development has followed a particular path, rather than making assumptions about individual behaviour or motivation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of a life factor (rather than a lifestyle choice)?
A) Choosing to follow a vegan diet
B) Deciding to take up regular swimming
C) Living in an overcrowded home in an area with high air pollution
D) Choosing to smoke cigarettes
practice_questions.marks: C) Living in an overcrowded home in an area with high air pollution [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two types of abuse identified in the specification.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for any two correctly named abuse types from the spec list:
• Physical, emotional, sexual, verbal, neglect, coercive control, financial (any two for the mark).

practice_questions.text: Give two ways that living in poverty can negatively affect a child's development.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for two genuinely different effects:
• Poor nutrition affecting physical growth and brain development (1)
• Damp or overcrowded housing increasing respiratory illness (1)
• Limited access to educational resources, affecting intellectual development (1)
• The stress of financial insecurity affecting emotional wellbeing (1)
• Reduced social participation due to inability to afford activities or clothing (1)
Do not credit near-identical points.

practice_questions.text: Explain how an authoritative parenting style can positively affect a child's social and emotional development.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
• Authoritative parenting combines high warmth with clear, explained rules (1).
• This means a child develops a secure sense of what is expected of them (1), therefore they are more likely to develop high self-esteem and good social skills because they feel valued and supported while learning appropriate boundaries (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe, with an example, how poor access to services can affect an individual's health and development across the lifespan.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. 2 marks for description; 2 marks for applied example.
• Access to services is a life factor affecting whether individuals can benefit from immunisations, mental health support, early years provision, or day centres (1). Where access is limited by geography, cost, or language barriers, individuals cannot receive the support that would maintain or improve their health (1).
• For example, an older adult in a rural area who has no transport and no nearby day centre may become severely socially isolated (1), meaning they lose regular social contact and stimulation that would support both their emotional and intellectual wellbeing (1).

practice_questions.text:
Sienna Okafor is 8 years old and lives with her mother in temporary housing in a damp, overcrowded flat. Her mother works long hours on a zero-hours contract and the family often relies on a food bank. Sienna has missed several immunisation appointments and has been absent from school frequently due to chest infections.

Using your knowledge of life factors, analyse how the life factors Sienna is experiencing are affecting her PIES development.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Identifies at least three distinct life factors accurately (e.g. economic/poverty, living environment, access to services). Chains each factor to its PIES impact and links impacts across domains. Consistently references Sienna's specific circumstances throughout.

Secure (5–6): Identifies two or three life factors with clear PIES links. Some chaining between domains. Generally accurate application to Sienna.

Developing (3–4): Accurate points listed but not chained. Life factors and lifestyle choices may be confused. Limited reference to Sienna.

Emerging (1–2): Basic points with little structure or accuracy.

Indicative content:
• Economic factor/poverty: zero-hours contract and food bank reliance → inadequate nutrition → impaired physical growth and brain development (P and I). Financial stress in the home may create an anxious, unsettled atmosphere affecting Sienna's emotional security (E).
• Living environment: damp, overcrowded flat → respiratory illness → physical health impact (P) → school absence → missed learning → falling behind peers intellectually (I) → reduced social contact with classmates (S).
• Access to services: missed immunisation appointments → higher risk of preventable illness (P), which compounds the cycle of school absence. Access to services is limited by the mother's working hours and transport difficulties.
• Chain: poverty → poor housing → chest infections → school absence → intellectual gaps → social isolation → lower self-esteem (E). These factors interact rather than operating in isolation.
• At age 8 (childhood stage), school attendance and peer relationships are particularly important for intellectual and social milestones — disruption at this stage has long-term consequences.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a 'life factor' from a 'lifestyle choice'?
options: A life factor is a behaviour the individual elects, such as diet or exercise
A life factor is a circumstance the individual is born into or finds themselves in, not a behaviour they choose
A life factor and a lifestyle choice are the same thing
A life factor only refers to genetic conditions

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of abuse involves a pattern of behaviour designed to control, threaten or frighten a person, often in a relationship?
The parenting style that combines high warmth with clear, explained rules and is associated with the most positive developmental outcomes is called _____ parenting.
Having two or more long-term health conditions at the same time is known as _____.
Match each life factor to its correct category:

flashcard_questions.q: What is a 'life factor' in health and social care?
flashcard_questions.a: A condition or circumstance an individual is born into or finds themselves in — not a behaviour they choose.

flashcard_questions.q: Name all seven types of abuse listed in the spec.
flashcard_questions.a: Physical, emotional, sexual, verbal, neglect, coercive control, financial.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between absolute poverty and relative poverty?
flashcard_questions.a: Absolute = lacking basic necessities to survive. Relative = having significantly less than the average living standard in society.

flashcard_questions.q: Which parenting style combines high warmth with clear, explained rules?
Which parenting style involves strict rules with low warmth and demands obedience without explanation?
What does 'comorbidity' mean in a health context?
flashcard_questions.a: Having two or more long-term health conditions at the same time in the same individual.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two environmental life factors that directly affect physical health.
flashcard_questions.a: Air pollution (respiratory illness) and overcrowded housing (infection spread and sleep disruption).

flashcard_questions.q: What UK review (2010) highlighted that inequalities in access to services drive health inequalities?
Why is bullying classified as an educational life factor rather than a lifestyle choice?
flashcard_questions.a: The child being bullied does not choose the bullying — it is imposed on them by others, affecting their development without consent.

flashcard_questions.q: How does coercive control affect a victim's social development?
flashcard_questions.a: The perpetrator enforces isolation from friends and family, cutting off social contacts and support networks.

flashcard_questions.q: What distinguishes a 'congenital' condition from a 'genetic' condition?
flashcard_questions.a: Congenital = present at birth (may or may not be inherited). Genetic = caused by inherited faulty genes passed from a parent.

glossary_terms.definition: A condition or circumstance that an individual is born into or finds themselves in, which influences their growth, development and health outcomes across the lifespan.
The extent to which an individual can make use of health, social care, and community services that support their growth, development, and well-being.
A person's enduring pattern of emotional, romantic, and/or sexual attraction to others, which may be a life factor influencing their experiences of discrimination or social support.
The co-occurrence of two or more long-term health conditions in the same individual, which can complicate diagnosis, treatment, and care planning.

items.title: Michael Marmot and the Social Determinants of Health
items.description: Professor Sir Michael Marmot explains how social conditions — employment, housing, education, access to services — determine health outcomes across the lifespan. Directly underpins the Marmot Review referenced in this lesson.

items.title: The Truth About Child Poverty — Professor Green Documentary
items.description: UK documentary showing how poverty as a life factor affects children's PIES development — covers housing, nutrition, education, and emotional wellbeing.

items.title: Britain's Extreme Poverty: Life in the UK's Forgotten Deprivation
items.description: Witness documentary on the lived reality of poverty in the UK — grounds the economic life factor in real human stories relevant to care practitioners.

items.title: 63 Up (2019)
items.description: Michael Apted's longitudinal series shows how life factors — class, geography, family structure, education — shape very different life trajectories from the same starting point.

items.title: Marmot Review 2010: Fair Society, Healthy Lives — The Health Foundation
items.description: Summary of the landmark Marmot Review on health inequalities in England — the primary academic source behind the access-to-services content in this lesson.

items.title: Age UK: Health inequalities and older people
items.description: Age UK's briefing on how life factors — poverty, isolation, housing — affect health outcomes specifically in later adulthood, relevant for practitioner understanding.

items.title: NHS: Health inequalities — what are they and why do they matter?
items.description: NHS England overview of health inequalities, explaining how access to services and socioeconomic factors drive different health outcomes — useful revision reference.

items.title: Skills for Care: Understanding the people we support
items.description: Skills for Care guidance on person-centred care, designed for adult social care workers — links Marmot-style life-factor awareness to day-to-day care practice.
